questions.stem: Which of the following best defines gross domestic product?
options: The total value of goods and services produced in a country in a year
The total income earned by a country's residents wherever they work
The total value of a country's exports in a year
The average income per person in a country
questions.why: GDP measures output produced within the country's borders over a year.
whyNot: That is closer to gross national income.
Exports are only one component of output.
That is GDP per capita.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines GDP per capita?
options: Gross domestic product divided by the population
Gross domestic product divided by the number of businesses
The growth rate of gross domestic product
Gross domestic product measured in a foreign currency
questions.why: Per capita means per head, and it is the figure to use when judging whether a product is affordable.
whyNot: The denominator is population, not the number of firms.
That is the economic growth rate.
Currency conversion does not make a figure per capita.

questions.stem: Which three components make up the human development index?
options: Income per head, life expectancy and years of schooling
Income per head, unemployment and inflation
GDP, exports and imports
Income per head, inequality and pollution
questions.why: Because it includes health and education, HDI measures whether growth has actually improved lives.
whyNot: Unemployment and inflation are macroeconomic indicators, not HDI components.
Those are all output and trade measures.
HDI excludes inequality and environmental quality, which is one of its limitations.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes an emerging economy?
options: An economy growing rapidly from a developing base, with rising incomes and expanding manufacturing
An economy with high income per head and a dominant service sector
An economy with low income per head and a dominant agricultural sector
An economy whose output is falling
questions.why: Emerging economies typically grow at several times the rate of developed ones and offer the fastest-growing consumer markets.
whyNot: That describes a developed economy.
That describes a developing economy.
A contracting economy is not what emerging means.

questions.stem: GDP is $48 billion and the population is 7.5 million. What is GDP per capita?
whyNot: That multiplies rather than divides.
That inverts the calculation.
That misplaces the decimal point by a factor of ten.

questions.stem: GDP rises from $50bn to $53bn. What is the growth rate?
whyNot: That is the increase in billions, not the percentage.
That divides by the new figure instead of the old one.
That expresses the ratio rather than the percentage change.

questions.stem: Which sector typically dominates a developed economy?
options: Services
Agriculture
Mining
Construction
questions.why: Developed economies have large tertiary sectors, while developing economies have large primary sectors.
whyNot: Agriculture dominates in developing economies.
Mining dominates only in particular resource economies.
Construction is a component of the secondary sector, not the dominant one.

questions.stem: Which type of product benefits most from rising incomes in an emerging economy?
options: A luxury good with high income elasticity of demand
A necessity with low income elasticity of demand
An inferior good with negative income elasticity
A good whose demand does not respond to income
questions.why: High income elasticity means demand rises proportionately more than income, so growth translates directly into sales.
whyNot: Demand for necessities rises only slightly as income rises.
Demand for inferior goods falls as income rises.
Zero income elasticity means growth brings no extra demand.

questions.stem: How does economic growth typically change employment patterns?
options: Labour moves out of agriculture into manufacturing and then into services
Labour moves out of services into agriculture
Employment patterns do not change as economies grow
All employment moves into the primary sector
questions.why: Urbanisation accelerates and skills demand rises, which is why skill shortages appear in exactly the roles growth creates.
whyNot: The shift runs in the opposite direction.
Structural change is one of the most consistent features of growth.
The primary sector shrinks as a share of employment.

questions.stem: Why does a low-cost production location tend not to stay low cost?
options: Growth raises wages, which erodes the cost advantage that attracted the investment
Governments always ban foreign investment eventually
Productivity falls as economies grow
Exchange rates always move against growing economies
questions.why: The location that is cheap today may not be cheap in ten years, which is a strong evaluative point in any location question.
whyNot: That is not a general pattern.
Productivity generally rises with growth, not falls.
Exchange rates do not move in a single predictable direction.

questions.stem: A country has a high GDP per capita but a very small, dispersed population. What is the likely conclusion for a consumer goods business?
options: Total market value is low and distribution costs are high, whatever the income figure suggests
The market is highly attractive because income per head is high
The business should assess the country only using HDI
Population size is irrelevant to market potential
questions.why: Market value is income per head multiplied by population, so a high income in a tiny population is a small market.
whyNot: Income per head alone does not make a market viable.
HDI is more useful for assessing a production location than a market.
Population is one of the two determinants of market size.

questions.stem: Why can a high GDP per capita coexist with widespread poverty?
options: An average says nothing about how income is distributed
GDP per capita is always measured inaccurately
Poverty is not related to income
GDP per capita excludes the wealthiest households
questions.why: Averages hide distribution, and for most consumer products the relevant market is an urban middle class rather than the whole population.
whyNot: The measurement is reasonable; the issue is what an average conceals.
Poverty is closely related to income; the point is its distribution.
It includes all income, which is part of why the average is raised.

questions.stem: Which measure would be most useful in assessing a country as a production location, and why?
options: HDI, because education and health predict the skills and reliability of the workforce
GDP, because total output shows how much can be produced
GDP per capita, because it shows what workers can afford to buy
The growth rate alone, because it shows the future
questions.why: For a location decision the workforce matters most, and HDI captures the health and education that underpin it.
whyNot: Total output says little about the workforce a business would employ.
Purchasing power matters for a market assessment, not a location one.
A growth rate alone tells you nothing about skills or infrastructure.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a limitation of GDP as an indicator?
options: It excludes the informal economy, which is large in many developing countries
It cannot be calculated for developing economies
It measures only exports
It is updated only once a decade
questions.why: GDP also says nothing about distribution and needs adjustment for differences in the cost of living.
whyNot: It is calculated for virtually every economy.
It measures total output, of which exports are one part.
It is published at least annually and usually quarterly.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a consequence of rapid economic growth for businesses selling in that country?
options: Spending shifts from necessities towards discretionary goods
Demand for all products falls equally
The number of competitors always falls
Exchange rates become fixed
questions.why: A rising middle class creates demand for goods previously unaffordable, which is the core opportunity growth presents.
whyNot: Growth raises demand, particularly for income-elastic products.
Growth generally attracts new entrants.
Growth does not fix exchange rates.

questions.stem: Why is high growth often described as volatile growth?
options: Fast-growing economies can contract sharply, so the risk is greater as well as the opportunity
High growth is always measured incorrectly
Growth rates above 5% are impossible to sustain for any period
Volatility only affects developed economies
questions.why: Naming the volatility alongside the opportunity is what turns a description of a growth rate into a judgement.
whyNot: Measurement is not the issue.
Some economies have sustained high growth for decades; the point is that it is less stable.
Emerging economies are typically more volatile, not less.
